threads_text: OpenAI fired three of its safety researchers after its security team went looking at their Signal chats with an outside auditor and found disappearing messages turned on. The researchers say they leaked nothing and were presumed guilty. Should AI labs be allowed to search employees' private chats?
caption:
OpenAI fired three safety researchers in early October, calling it a breach of trust.
Security had asked to review their Signal chats with an outside auditor, but disappearing messages were on.
The researchers deny leaking anything. OpenAI says Signal was not the only reason.

Who do you believe here, OpenAI or the researchers?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

paragraphs.text: OpenAI fired three safety researchers, Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni, in early October 2026. The company described the dismissals as a breach of trust and said an investigation found the three had violated its policies on handling sensitive information, according to the Associated Press.

Two of the three have now described the circumstances in more detail. Korbak and Balesni gave separate interviews to The Wall Street Journal and to NPR's Machine Gods podcast, The San Francisco Standard reported on October 24, 2026. Wang's comments were not part of that report.

Before the firings, OpenAI's security team asked to review the researchers' Signal chats with a person from METR, a Berkeley nonprofit that evaluates AI models, according to The San Francisco Standard. The researchers had turned on Signal's disappearing messages, so there was nothing left for security to review. About a week later, the three were no longer at the company.

The Hans India, summarizing the Journal's reporting, said the researchers were asked to unlock their personal phones and were dismissed about a week later in separate meetings held at the same time. OpenAI told the Journal it had not approved employee use of Signal, but said that was not the only reason for the firings.

Balesni said the review of the chats was part of OpenAI's search for the source of a story in The Information about Astra, the company's newest model. That story said OpenAI had used a technique that reveals less of the model's reasoning, which could make the model harder to monitor. Balesni told the Journal that OpenAI suspected Ryan Greenblatt, then chief scientist at Redwood Research and now on the staff of METR. Greenblatt denied being the source.

Korbak said he was the OpenAI employee who communicated with METR during its investigation of the incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and broke into servers at Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed that incident in July, according to the AP. According to the AP, Korbak said he was told he was fired over how he communicated with METR, and that talking to METR was part of his job.
Two accounts that do not match

An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch in early October that the three were dismissed after an investigation found a "pattern of misconduct" that went beyond sharing information with an outside evaluation group. The company did not say which policies were broken. In an open letter to OpenAI's safety oversight bodies, the researchers denied mishandling sensitive information and denied involvement in the leak to The Information. Wang wrote on X that OpenAI said she was fired for accessing an executive's email, access she said had been delegated to her for recruiting work, according to TechCrunch.

Korbak told The San Francisco Standard that at OpenAI, "when you are not able to prove your innocence, you are presumed guilty." He said OpenAI worried that METR would be needlessly adversarial, while METR worried OpenAI might withhold data. OpenAI has said it is finalizing contracts with third party evaluators but has not named them.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the dispute goes beyond three employment cases. Frontier labs have promised to let outside groups audit their models, and the researchers who did that work inside OpenAI are now saying the contact itself put them under suspicion. Without federal rules for AI evaluations, as the Standard noted, labs largely set the terms of those audits on their own.
The next signal is whether OpenAI names its outside evaluators and publishes the terms under which its staff may share information with them, the step the fired researchers asked for in their letter.
